summary: For ages 7–8, help children sort familiar Earth events onto a fast↔slow timescale using evidence, without quantifying the timescales. Fast events (earthquakes, volcanic eruptions) cause big changes within seconds to days that people can watch happen, though some eruptions continue on and off for months or years. Slow processes (erosion, canyon carving, mountain building) take far longer than a lifetime to make big changes, even if small bits of wearing-away can sometimes be seen. Make slow change believable with before/after image pairs and time-lapse, and have children justify each classification from several sources (text, images, video). The target insight is that 'the land changes' and 'the land changes slowly' are both true.
misconceptions: All changes to the land are slow and gradual — or, conversely, that landscapes are permanent and never change.
Fast events (earthquakes) and slow processes (erosion) are the same kind of thing.
Mountains, canyons and coastlines have 'always been there' as they are now.
Slow processes are not really happening because you cannot see them move.

activities.title: Drag-and-play fast↔slow timescale line
steps: Place each Earth event (earthquake, volcanic eruption, river carving a canyon, a rising mountain, a cliff slowly worn back by waves) onto a line labelled from 'seconds' at one end to 'millions of years' at the other.

Play each event: a fast event like an earthquake is shown at about real speed and jolts the ground almost at once, while a slow one like a canyon deepening only becomes visible after you scrub a 'millions of years' control and watch the river do its slow work — this is a sped-up, compressed model of the slow process, not real time.
Put an earthquake and a canyon side by side on the line and describe, in your own words, how they are at opposite ends.

For each event you called 'slow', name a piece of evidence (rock layers built up over time, worn stone, a time-lapse made from real photos of a cliff or riverbank) that shows the change happens gradually over a long time; remember the sped-up canyon animation is a model, not evidence by itself.
activities.insight: Both fast events and slow processes reshape the land, but fast ones make big changes in moments to days while slow ones take far longer than a lifetime; being unable to watch a whole change happen does not mean it is not happening.

activities.title: Before/after detective with a tappable landscape
steps: Explore a landscape and tap features — a volcano erupting, a fault that slipped during an earthquake, a canyon, a cliff slowly worn back by waves — to reveal whether each change was fast or slow along with a before/after image pair (photos for quick changes; drawings or reconstructions for changes too slow to photograph).
For each feature, say out loud what is different between the 'before' and 'after' pictures.
Decide whether that change could happen quickly or only over a very long time, and explain how you decided.
activities.insight: Paired images of the same place show that landscapes are not permanent; some features changed quickly and others changed over a time far longer than a lifetime.

activities.title: Evidence-based sort and sequence
steps: Sort a set of events into two columns: rapid events vs slow processes.
Give at least two examples of your own for each column (e.g. earthquake, volcanic eruption, landslide, flood for fast; erosion, mountain formation, canyon carving for slow).
Order the events by roughly how long they take, from quickest to slowest, without stating exact times.
For the slow processes, point to evidence (rock strata, worn rock, a time-lapse made from real photos) that shows the change is real; a sped-up animation is a model, not evidence by itself.
Apply the rule to a brand-new event you have not seen before: fast or slow, and how do you know?
activities.insight: A useful test for 'fast or slow' is whether the whole change could be watched happening from start to finish, not how dramatic it looks; evidence can support a slow process even when you cannot see it move.

checkQuestion: A river carves a deep canyon, and a volcano erupts. One of these changes the land quickly and one very slowly. Which is which — and how do you know?
checkAnswer: The volcanic eruption is the quick change (you could watch it happen in hours or days); the river carving the canyon is the slow change (it takes far longer than anyone could watch — many thousands or millions of years). The test is whether you could see the change happening.
